top_signals.title: Where Soldiers Enjoyed Thanksgiving
top_signals.summary:
Today, I’m slicing turkey. Grease dots my pinks and greens. Scuffs mar my jump boots. As I serve, soldiers feast: smoked turkey, honey-glazed ham, a steamship round of beef, smoked flank steak, and a whole smoked pig. Alongside those entrees, they’re enjoying collard greens, cornbread twice over, baked mac and cheese, shrimp cocktail, deviled eggs, and three gravies. Families of our young soldiers eat for just $8.75. Others, $11.85. The U.S. Army does Thanksgiving well.  While the ideal American Thanksgiving finds everyone back at the family home, I’ve only had four of those in almost 20 years. top_signals.title: How does EIA compare different types of energy?
top_signals.summary: To compare production and consumption across different resources, we convert to a common energy metric, British thermal units (Btu), which typically measures the heat content of the fuels such as petroleum, natural gas, and coal that are burned for energy. For energy sources such as hydropower, wind, solar, and geothermal that aren't combusted to create energy, we apply a constant conversion factor based on the heat content of electricity.
